title: Platform infrastructure: Convenience can deepen private control
desc: Treats platforms as social infrastructure shaped by data, network effects and interconnection power, not neutral marketplaces.

kps.k: Platforms organise essential services and social institutions, rather than merely connect buyers and sellers.
kps.d: The cluster frames platform power as control over the infrastructure through which others interact. Van Dijck, Poell and de Waal argue that platforms converge with existing institutions and reshape social practices. Plantin and colleagues describe a two-way transformation: infrastructures adopt platform business models while platforms become essential infrastructure. Both accounts challenge technology-only explanations; Plantin and colleagues also connect the shift to privatisation and deregulation. Their support consists of conceptual synthesis, historical argument and illustrative cases, not quantified causal tests.

qs.q: Platforms, in our view, do not cause a revolution; instead, they are gradually infiltrating in, and converging with, the (offline, legacy) institutions and practices through which democratic societies are organized.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

qs.q: We argue that the rise of digital technologies, in a neoliberal, political, and economic climate, has simultaneously facilitated a “platformization” of infrastructures and an “infrastructuralization” of platforms.
qs.a: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook · Academia · 2018

kps.k: Data extraction, network effects and control of interconnection can reinforce concentrated market power.
kps.d: The supplied Platform Capitalism account presents Srnicek’s explanation of how network effects, cross-subsidised services and sustained engagement expand opportunities to extract data and accumulate capital. Plantin and colleagues add that platform owners can recruit independent developers while retaining central control and discouraging interoperability with competitors. The Platform Society locates disproportionate infrastructural power in Alphabet-Google, Apple, Facebook, Amazon and Microsoft within the Western ecosystem. Claims of almost perpetual monopolistic returns remain conceptual propositions, not measured outcomes or established forecasts.

qs.q: Finally, because achieving lock-in is among platform builders’ principal goals, most actively discourage the construction of gateways—to borrow an infrastructure studies concept—which might permit interoperability with competitors.
qs.a: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook · Academia · 2018

qs.q: The Western ecosystem is mostly operated by a handful of big tech companies (Alphabet-Google, Apple,  Facebook, Amazon, and Microsoft) whose infrastructural services are central to the ecosystem’s overall design and the distribution of data flows.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

kps.k: Modular innovation and user benefits can coexist with dependency and private control.
kps.d: Plantin and colleagues acknowledge that reusable infrastructure lowers development costs and enables third-party innovation. Google Maps illustrates the exchange: developers gain programmable mapping, while Google receives activity data and extends its branded interface. Developers can nevertheless face mandatory updates, design constraints and the expense of maintaining versions for competing platforms. The authors contrast the Open Web’s publicly accessible standards with Facebook-controlled transactions, while noting that APIs also support government open data. Their argument therefore concerns ownership and governance, not an inherently restrictive technology.

qs.q: As with Facebook, the principal benefits to Google are the user activity data returned by the API and the ubiquity of its branded interface, while the myriad applications connected to the Google platform benefit from the ability to build on Google-provided data.
qs.a: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook · Academia · 2018

qs.q: The costs of this approach, as platform studies has shown, come in the form of constraints, constant revisions forced by platform updates, and lock-in to the platform’s conception of users, functionality, and design values.
qs.a: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook · Academia · 2018

kps.k: The main analytical tension concerns whether business incentives sufficiently explain platform conduct.
kps.d: The Platform Capitalism source praises an economic account that treats technology companies’ actions as responses to business needs rather than cultural values or political motives. The Platform Society explicitly rejects an exclusively economic explanation and examines how algorithms, interfaces, ownership and user agreements jointly govern interactions. Plantin and colleagues combine business architecture with infrastructure history and public-service concerns. This is a difference in explanatory emphasis, not a documented direct exchange or a disagreement about whether commercial incentives matter.

qs.q: Specifically, by positioning major tech companies as ‘economic actors within a capitalist mode of production’ (3) – instead of cultural or political actors who are informed by cultural values or motivated by the pursuit of power – readers come to understand, with economic clarity, that these companies’ actions are merely reactions to business needs.
We agree that online platforms are at the core of an important development, but we think of them neither as an exclusive economic phenomenon nor as a technological construct with social corollaries.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

kps.k: Private convenience does not establish collective benefit or resolve responsibility for public provision.
kps.d: The Platform Society acknowledges benefits such as inexpensive accommodation and host income but asks who funds safety enforcement, street cleaning and educational production. These examples raise questions about allocating costs and responsibilities rather than demonstrate net social harm. Plantin and colleagues similarly balance Google’s financing capacity and reduced duplication against concentrated control over knowledge. Their public-service comparison remains qualified: universal provision was historically an imperfect ideal, and their discussion of US Internet access highlights continued exclusion of low-income users.

qs.q: The connective qualities of online platforms, however, do not automatically translate into public values.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

qs.q: Second, the ability not only to access all that knowledge but also to build upon Google’s code avoids redundant effort and expense.
qs.a: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook · Academia · 2018

kps.k: Practical governance requires sector-specific scrutiny of access, accountability and competing public values.
kps.d: The Platform Society recommends assessing privacy contextually and treating fairness, solidarity, transparency and democratic control alongside consumer protection. These values can conflict, including when law-enforcement transparency threatens privacy. Its Facebook and Airbnb examples also qualify any deterministic account: users, public criticism and regulatory demands can change platform rules. Plantin and colleagues propose comparative research on exclusion and policy alternatives across sectors, rather than assume a fixed trajectory. Together, the accounts direct attention to who controls essential services, who bears their costs and who can contest their rules.

qs.q: Privacy issues have been a bone of contention between platform owners, state regulators, watchdog organizations, citizens, and lawyers; and they need to be assessed contextually—that means, in the specific context of each application in each social situation in each specific sector (Nissenbaum 2010).
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

qs.q: In all cases, scholars of infrastructure could attend to the technological influences and policy alternatives that tip the delicate balance between the public interest and corporate power.
qs.a: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook · Academia · 2018

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources support the proposition that platforms function as consequential social infrastructure and that their convenience and innovative capacity can deepen private control. Their common reasoning is that platforms organise interactions through data extraction, network effects, APIs, ownership rules and control over interoperability; as platforms become embedded in essential institutions and services, these mechanisms can create dependency, lock-in and concentrated power. The sources also consistently distinguish user or developer benefits from collective benefit, treating convenience as compatible with pressure on public values and public-service obligations. Material variation concerns explanatory scope rather than the core proposition: the Platform Capitalism account foregrounds capitalist business incentives and monopolistic returns, whereas The Platform Society and Plantin and colleagues use broader institutional, historical and public-value frameworks incorporating regulation, privatisation, social norms and competing values. Plantin and colleagues place particular emphasis on the dual character of modularity, which lowers innovation costs while preserving central corporate control. These are principally conceptual syntheses, historical arguments and illustrative cases rather than quantified causal tests, and this curated set should not be treated as representative of academia generally.

qs.q: Platforms, in our view, do not cause a revolution; instead, they are gradually infiltrating in, and converging with, the (offline, legacy) institutions and practices through which democratic societies are organized.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

elens.an: Across this curated 2015–2022 selection, the sources support the proposition that platforms function as consequential social and economic infrastructure rather than neutral marketplaces, and that convenience, innovation and connectivity can deepen private control. Their common reasoning is that platforms govern interactions through data extraction, network effects, technical architecture and control over interconnection, producing dependency, lock-in and concentrated power. They also agree that user or developer benefits do not by themselves establish public benefit. Material variation lies chiefly in explanatory scope: the Platform Capitalism account foregrounds capitalist business incentives and monopolistic returns, whereas The Platform Society and Plantin and colleagues embed commercial incentives within broader institutional, political, sociocultural and public-value governance. Plantin and colleagues most explicitly balance modular innovation and lower development costs against corporate control; The Platform Society gives greater weight to contested values, sector-specific regulation and the capacity of users and public pressure to alter platform rules. These differences qualify and develop the shared account without opposing its principal proposition; the curated sources should not be treated as representative of all work from the period.

qs.q: Platforms, in our view, do not cause a revolution; instead, they are gradually infiltrating in, and converging with, the (offline, legacy) institutions and practices through which democratic societies are organized.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018
